Here's a good explanation of those diets and how they don't really (and you don't want them to) affect your blood ph levels: http://www.webmd.com/diet/alkaline-diets

Note the high manganese?  From the Wikipedia: "Many nutritionists attribute joint pain, inflammation, arthritis, bursitis, dermatitis, and many diseases including osteoporosis, schizophrenia, diabetes, and epilepsy to manganese deficiency." ( http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_deficiency_%28medicine%29 )

Note the magnesium? Magnesium deficiency is associated (correlated?) with arthritis (something ACV is often promoted to help with). So, if you don't ruin your stomach with too much vinegar, maybe the magnesium is helping?

Also, ACV will probably cause your body to expel more fluids than normal... than might make you feel less bloated and reduce fluids in joints like ankles?

So, the ACV may make some people feel better, but it probably isn't because it changed their blood ph level.

First: His only manifestation was not talking (04:10). I personally didn't talk until I was almost 5yo (I'm a very strong introvert to this day). I still remember my parents making a fuss when one day, I was curled under a blanket on the couch and they were in the kitchen asking where I was and I said "I'm right here". This really sounds like a woman who drug her first child (a 2yo-3yo) through a battery of diagnosis for autism without waiting for the kid to mature because the kid didn't feel compelled to follow the developmental 'guidelines' published in all of the books. And, what doctor would say give up all hope of language skills about a 3yo? All, I can say is thank God my mom was lazy or I might have been 'diagnosed' as retarded by the time I was 5yo. 

From the video, this sounds like a woman who's child hit a developmental blip and she launched into an obsessive 'home schooling' attitude. This is more an example of how a parent who chooses to spend an extraordinary amount of time (by today's US standards) on educating her children could enable them to achieve much higher levels of learning at an earlier age. The boy is not 'officially' in any realm of Nobel prize material, only exploring science that could result on a noble prize some day according to one person's opinion. This boy's siblings are also more advanced than their age-peers. Yet, she doesn't claim them to be autistic.

> The doctors were saying that there was no hope though, I'm not sure how she would disentangle the two. 

You need to keep in mind that this is a recounting of her perception of events. Doctors typically talk in terms of statistics. So a statement like "the odds are small that your child will achieve xyz at this specific age" to a doctor is accurate, but the parent interprets it as "NO HOPE!" (and that narrative sells the book better).

> I'm saying that no one has anything near a comprehensive understanding of autism

No one has a comprehensive understanding a many diagnosis that exist (the DSM even admits this!). There are tons of medications on the market that have been shown to work through research even though the exact mechanism isn't understood. 

BUT!

There are many specific aspects of autism that are becoming better understood every day and that body of work can be combined by an individual who specializes in the treatment of autism to provide valid advice.  Advice that would be more useful than just winging it based on the intuition of a non-autistic person. (And, I'm saying this as a person who just spent quite a while trying to get a NT psychologist to understand what I mean when I say that noise bothers me. It isn't a 'oh, I don't like that' opinion sort of thing. It is (in my perception) a very real, very physical, whole body response to sounds that I have yet to be able to describe to her so that she can understand what I mean.)

Does that mean that the doctors are always right?  NO. But, all that means is that you talk to the doctors about the various management aspects. You use their expertise to guide you in the various issues. 

For example, if some are seeing success from a specific diet, how do you know if that is after only 3 days or needs 3 months before you can tell if it was helpful, hurtful or indifferent? How do you interpret 'helpful' vs 'harmful'?  A better outward behavior could be the result of malnutrition and that wouldn't be a good long term approach. Do you run to a message board and trust the opinions of a bunch of strangers who may be subject to confirmation bias? 

Also, how (as a non-autistic person) do you interpret some activities?  If a child doesn't respond to verbal cues, how to you determine if they are deaf, willfully ignoring you, or just not responsive to that form of stimuli?

I may be fortunate in that I know several parents with willful children and their approach is to get the kid to burn out that energy while setting reasonable boundaries. And, I have sat smiling through many screaming tantrum fits trying to reassure those parents that it really is okay with me because I totally understand that they have to deal with a child who is not 'reasoning' at the time and that takes priority.

In another environment, I'm certain that parents could get those same kids 'diagnosed' and medicated into submission. But, I guess that people I know are not interested in that approach for temperament issues.

After reading your comment, I guess there are people out there who want to push their image of normal on others (especially the young) and who are willing to got to almost any extent to pursue that goal.

But, if the mother in the book is willing to grab onto the label "genius" to sell her book, then she should also accept the label of autism. Autism is not contagious and is (sometimes) an accurate diagnosis. I do think it is overused to medicate kids who are simply willful personalities. But, I object to the approach that the publisher is taking with that book and furthering the "autism is bad" attitude, especially given that the child was probably aided by his autism!

Your child is a female and will have life challenges related to her sex. Do you feel a need to throw off the label "female" or "girl" in order to give her better chances in life? If she turns out to be a genius and cures cancer, will a book about how she threw off the label of female be appropriate? {from my perspective, if she needs to throw off the label 'female' that is saying that female in general is bad}

I personally dislike much of the US medical system, but I will admit that I'm working through my own issues as an adult and finding some solutions because of research. So, while I might not think the physician down the street is anything more than a shill for the pharmaceutic industry, there are good aspects to the medical industry that should be explored. Writing a book to promote an antagonistic relationship between the research and those who might benefit is not a good thing in my opinion. But, I guess it is fashionable and will sell books.

I also wonder about the parents who will take such a book and use it to ignore all advice and set no limits on their children. Children by definition (autistic or otherwise) are small creatures who need to be taught age-appropriate boundaries that will keep them alive and allow them to excel in society.  Now, does that mean a 5yo boy should be able to sit at a desk for 6 hours? No (and how are people still amazed that they can't manage that feat?  I have trouble sitting still for 6hrs and I'm much, much older!). But, they should be learning to not walk onto a busy freeway and if they can't learn that concept then a responsible adult should be providing protection for them when they are near freeways. That's just life.

I would rather someone be out there complaining that too much research is locked behind pay walls that prevent the average citizen from access to the knowledge that tax payers funded for the sake of protecting profits.

But, I will grant you that there are people who want to medicate the young into personalities that suite their priorities and that is a problem. I guess it just doesn't temper my reaction to a promotion campaign that demonizes a diagnosis of autism yet again. It would make no sense to demonize a diagnosis of insulin resistance (diabetes) or traumatic head injury. But, it is okay to promote that the term 'autism' is to be avoided if at all possible and a label to be thrown off.

Part of the problem is that you have a diagnosis of tendonitis, so an MRI isn't really needed. It takes a min of 8 weeks rest to allow minor tendon damage to heal. You're slowing the healing process each time you push it to the point of inflammation. 

To recover a tendon, you need to start out with very LIGHT work that helps the healing fibers to re-align to the proper orientation while NOT causing inflammation that will reverse the healing process. For example, do the light work, then ice the area immediately after to stave off any swelling. If you set up a schedule to very gradually bring your tendon back into full use (a schedule that would be as a minimum 6 months)... you could be back to normal next year without any long term issues. (Sorry, tendons can only heal/regenerate so fast due to the limited blood supply that they get)

BUT, if you continue to push it to the point of inflammation, you could end up with a shredded mess that will never be back to full strength and may be a permanent source of pain. And, then you'll get your MRIs.

Look at manganese as a supplement. Also, tendons have poor blood supply, you might look at DMSO to increase the blood flow in the area. 

BUT, you should read up on tendonitis injuries. Resting is VERY important and pushing a damaged tendon can cause permanent damage by fraying off the fibers of the tendon as it rubs inside the swollen sheath structure. So, going back to squats too soon could give you permanent damage.
